intro: Ivan Ilić recorded this prelude in Paris in April 2006. Compare the spacing of the opening fifths with the weight of the later chordal statements, then follow the melody as it returns quietly.
question: How does Ilić separate a chord’s attack from its resonance?

sections.label: The first emergence
sections.mNote: rising figures acquire a more continuous accompaniment

sections.label: The quiet echo
sections.mNote: chordal melody returns quietly above an oscillating bass

cues.title: Space around the fifths
cues.text: In Ilić’s opening, attend to the gaps between the rising groups of notes. Debussy’s bare fifths leave room for resonance rather than immediately presenting a full major or minor chord.
cues.evidence: The work account describes the opening fifths: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie. The analysis shows sparse attacks, 0.6–1.2 per second, in the first 25 seconds; no pedal action is identified.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sustained first rise
cues.text: Across this stretch, the recorded level rises through several phrases rather than reaching its crest at once. Follow the growing continuity below the upper line as the music emerges from the quiet opening.
cues.evidence: The report shows relative level rising from −23.5 dB at 0:50 to −6.0 dB at 1:20, with structural boundaries at 1:00, 1:14 and 1:24. The score supplies the accompanying triplet motion, not an exact bar timestamp.

cues.title: Chords across the crest
cues.text: Ilić’s first broad crest extends beyond a single attack. Listen for the top line continuing through the thick chords, and for the decay of one sonority beneath the next.
cues.evidence: The 1:35, 1:40, 1:50 and 2:05 windows are among the report’s five highest-level windows. The broad chordal writing is described in the cited work account; these are within-recording measurements, not loudness comparisons with Meyer.

cues.title: The pressure falls away
cues.text: After the sustained chordal span, the sound retreats into a much quieter passage. Hear the withdrawal as part of the phrase rather than as an immediate stop.
cues.evidence: A boundary occurs at 2:42; relative level falls from −8.8 dB at 2:25 to −33.6 dB at 2:45 and −34.3 dB at 2:50.

cues.title: A second shorter swell
cues.text: The later ascent forms a separate swell, followed by another retreat. Compare its shape with the long first crest, without treating the two passages as identical music.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −27.3 dB at 3:00 to −12.4 dB at 3:30, then falls to −30.2 dB at 3:55. This describes the recorded contour, not an inferred tempo change.

cues.title: Melody heard as echo
cues.text: Through this later passage, Debussy’s chordal melody returns quietly, lower in the keyboard. Follow its outline above the oscillating bass and compare the resonance with the earlier statement.
cues.evidence: The score account identifies the lower, quiet return at bar 72. The 4:04 boundary and subsequent −22 to −20 dB span support passage-level placement; no score bar is aligned to this exact second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the last attacks
cues.text: The closing resonance continues after the remaining attacks have become sparse. Let that decay finish before comparing the ending with another pianist’s.
cues.evidence: The 5:05 window has 0.2 detected attacks per second; the 5:10–5:20 windows have none. Relative level falls from −28.7 dB at 5:00 to −53.4 dB at 5:15; this does not identify a precise pedal release.

transitions.title: The accompaniment gains continuity
transitions.how: The rising figures persist while a more continuous accompaniment starts the first expansion. The written move into B major changes the harmonic ground without discarding the opening’s upward contour.
transitions.evidence: The 1:00 analysis boundary and rise through 1:20 locate the passage. The B-major harmony and triplets come from the work account’s discussion of bars 16–21, not the machine key estimate.

transitions.title: The rising line acquires chordal weight
transitions.how: The ascent leads into a broad chordal span: the melody is carried by chord tops rather than isolated notes. Listen across the preparation and statement, not for a single precisely aligned arrival.
transitions.evidence: The 1:24 novelty boundary precedes the sustained high-level span at 1:35–2:25. The score’s preparation and broad chords support the general description; 84 seconds is not asserted to be bar 28.

transitions.title: The chordal span sheds its weight
transitions.how: The broad statement recedes before a quieter melodic fragment starts the next ascent. Reduced weight and more exposed line separate this passage from the preceding chords.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 2:42; the 2:45–2:50 windows are among the quietest in the report, after the high 2:25 window. The score account describes the transition and renewed fragment.

transitions.title: The chordal tune returns quietly
transitions.how: The later ascent subsides and the earlier chordal melody returns in a lower register. Its quiet setting over an oscillating bass changes the relationship between melodic line and resonance.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 4:04 follows the 3:30–3:55 rise and retreat. The lower quiet echo and oscillating bass are written features described in the work account; timing remains approximate.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
